query: Earlier automotive-catalyst research reported that Cu–Ni catalysts can oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts can resist poisoning by H2O and NO and enable oxidation below 150 °C. Multi-principal-element catalysts in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been explored as a framework for combining high activity, thermal stability, and reduced platinum-group-metal use. These prior results demonstrate individual capabilities but do not establish the combined performance demanded by increasingly stringent regulations: clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime despite the mileage-related degradation observed in real-driving-emission studies. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention, explaining how it would work, predicting the change relative to the unmodified catalyst, defining the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, citing supporting prior evidence, and specifying an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled surface dealloying treatment that selectively removes less noble elements (e.g., Ni) from the near‐equiatomic multi-principal-element catalyst will enrich the surface in Cu (with retained minimal Pd/Pt), thus enhancing low-temperature oxidation activity, improving resistance to H2O and NO poisoning, and leading to better long-term durability under simulated automotive exhaust and aging conditions compared to the untreated catalyst.
generation.material_initial_state: Near‐equiatomic multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst containing Cu, Ni, minimal amounts of Pd/Pt, and other co-alloying elements.
generation.intervention: Apply a mild chemical or electrochemical dealloying treatment that selectively leaches out less noble elements such as Ni.
generation.conditions: Testing under transient, low-temperature automotive exhaust conditions (approximately 100–150 °C with exposure to H2O, NO, CO, and hydrocarbons) combined with an accelerated aging regimen simulating vehicle lifetime thermal cycling and surface sintering.
generation.structural_mediator: A restructured surface exhibiting nanoparticulate clusters enriched in Cu (and maintained minimal but well-dispersed Pd/Pt) that form robust oxide interfaces to resist sintering and poisoning.
generation.mechanism: Selective dealloying promotes surface segregation by removing less catalytically beneficial elements, thereby enriching the surface in Cu and minimal Pd/Pt. This rearrangement creates stable catalytic sites which lower the oxidation onset temperature, improve poisoning resistance, and enhance durability under thermal cycling.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified catalyst, the dealloyed sample should exhibit a lower light‐off temperature for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation, sustained activity in the presence of H2O and NO, and reduced structural degradation or sintering after accelerated aging.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics of the untreated near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element catalyst under identical transient low-temperature and aging conditions.
generation.boundary: The benefits of the dealloying treatment are anticipated to be effective under typical automotive exhaust compositions and temperatures (approximately 100–300 °C). Conditions that fall significantly outside this range (e.g., very high temperatures or non-standard exhaust gas mixtures) may not yield the same performance improvements.
generation.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty regarding the quantitative extent of performance improvement under variable real-world conditions and how closely the accelerated aging tests mimic actual vehicle lifetime degradation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of catalysts: one set remains as the original untreated near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element catalyst, and the other set undergoes the controlled dealloying treatment. Both sets will be subjected to simulated automotive exhaust conditions at low temperatures with varying gas compositions (including H2O, NO, CO, and hydrocarbons) and accelerated thermal aging cycles designed to simulate high mileage.
measurements: Measurement of light‐off (ignition) temperatures for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation.
Evaluation of conversion efficiency in the presence of poisoning agents (H2O and NO).
Structural and compositional analysis using techniques such as TEM and XPS to assess surface enrichment and sintering before and after aging.
Long-term activity retention and stability metrics under repeated thermal cycling.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the dealloyed catalysts do not show a statistically significant lowering of the light‐off temperature, fail to maintain higher conversion efficiencies in the presence of poisoning agents, or exhibit comparable or greater degradation in structure and activity relative to the untreated catalysts under the specified test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: A controlled, selective surface dealloying treatment that removes a portion of the less noble elements (e.g., Ni) from the near‐equiatomic multi-principal-element catalyst can lead to surface enrichment of Cu and trace amounts of Pd/Pt. This enriched surface structure will simultaneously lower the light-off temperature for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation, enhance resistance to poisoning by H2O and NO, and improve long-term durability under aging while keeping overall platinum-group-metal usage low.
drafts.material_initial_state: A near‐equiatomic multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst containing Cu, Ni, Pd/Pt (in minimal amounts), and other co-alloyed elements.
drafts.intervention: Apply a mild chemical (or electrochemical) dealloying treatment that selectively leaches out more reactive or less catalytically beneficial elements such as Ni, thereby enriching the surface in Cu and residual Pd/Pt.
drafts.conditions: Catalyst operating under transient and low-temperature conditions typical of automotive exhaust (e.g., 100–150 °C under exposure to H2O, NO, CO, and hydrocarbons) and an accelerated aging regimen representative of vehicle lifetime (e.g., thermal cycling and surface sintering over simulated high-mileage conditions).
drafts.structural_mediator: A restructured surface comprised of nanoparticulate clusters with a higher local concentration of Cu and minimal but well-dispersed Pd/Pt, which forms robust oxide interfaces that resist sintering and poisoning.
drafts.mechanism: The dealloying treatment promotes selective surface segregation: by removing a portion of the less noble (and potentially less active) elements, the remaining surface is enriched in components (Cu and minimal Pd/Pt) that are already known to favor low-temperature oxidation and poison resistance. This adjustment in surface composition creates more stable catalytic sites that are less prone to structural degradation under thermal cycling, while maintaining low overall PGM content.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified catalyst, the dealloyed catalyst is expected to show a lower oxidation onset (light‐off) temperature for CO and hydrocarbons, maintain activity in the presence of typical exhaust poisons (H2O and NO), and exhibit reduced degradation or sintering after accelerated aging tests.
drafts.baseline: Performance metrics of the untreated near‐equiatomic multi-principal-element catalyst under the same (transient, low-temperature, poisoned, and aging) conditions.
drafts.boundary: The intervention is anticipated to be effective under conditions where the operating temperatures remain within 100–300 °C and for exhaust gas compositions similar to typical automotive emissions. Extreme conditions beyond these ranges (e.g., very high temperatures or non-standard gas mixtures) may not yield the same benefits.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of catalysts: one set of the original near-equiatomic multi-principal-element catalysts and a second set that has undergone the controlled dealloying treatment. Subject both sets to simulated automotive-exhaust flow conditions at low temperatures with oscillating gas compositions (including H2O, NO, CO, and hydrocarbons) and conduct accelerated thermal aging cycles (simulated mileage aging).
measurements: Light-off temperature (ignition temperature) measurements for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation.
Activity retention (conversion efficiency) in the presence of poisoning agents (H2O and NO).
Structural and compositional analysis (using TEM, XPS) pre- and post-aging to evaluate surface enrichment and sintering.
Long-term stability metrics under repeated thermal cycling.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the dealloyed catalysts do not show a statistically significant decrease in the light-off temperature, fail to better maintain conversion efficiency in the presence of poisons, or exhibit comparable/diminished durability or structural degradation compared to the untreated baseline catalysts under the designated test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.
